audit.recode_to: From 'lexical' to predictable, morphologically anchored stress (Colombian Siona, Wheeler 1987 I:89-91): primary stress on the final syllable of the base/root (σ2 of 2-syll, σ3 of 3-syll; σ2+σ4 strongest in 4-syll bases, i.e. iambic within the base), all base syllables bearing some stress, suffixes/enclitics alternating unstressed-stressed after the base, a few lexically stressed suffixes. In catalog terms: kind = morphological/stem-final (dom = stem, right edge), not lexical; whole-word positional rule still not count-computable ('None ridable' over the word can stand) because suffix strings vary. Add a caution that Ecuadorian Siona (Bruil 2014:86-87) shows only a word-final pitch rise with no demonstrated stress system, so the languoid mixes two differently described varieties. The StressTyp2 'initial' contra note remains valid (neither 1962 nor 1987 supports fixed initial stress).
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim at Wheeler & Wheeler 1962:107-108 in the held PDF (rendered PDF pp. 12-13). (2) The deciding source is a 1962 SIL phonemics article with a one-paragraph, morphology-blind stress section; the same author's 1987 reference grammar (held but unused: §2.2.3 pp. 89-92, read now from page images hi-105..108) analyses stress as predictable from the base: strongest stress base-final (iambic σ2/σ4 in 4-syll bases), alternating rhythm over suffixes, stress 'rarely' meaning-distinguishing. That directly undercuts the 'lexical' classification, which was inferred from the 1962 list of three surface patterns (those patterns are base+atonic-suffix vs. disyllabic-base parses under the 1987 analysis). Bruil 2014 §3.2.3 (held) adds that Ecuadorian Siona has no demonstrated stress system, only a word-final pitch rise. (3)

sources.quote: No minimal stress/tone pairs known; 'The regular prosodic pattern in the language is that the pitch goes up in the last syllable of the word'; no conclusive evidence for a contrastive stress or tone system in Ecuadorian Siona; Colombian Siona described as a stress language by Wheeler 1970:20-21, 1987b:89-92.

sources.quote: Base ('forma básica') of 1-4 syllables, all stressed; strongest stress on σ2 of disyllabic bases, on the last σ of trisyllabic bases (σ2 > σ1), on σ2 and σ4 of quadrisyllabic bases; monosyllabic bases stressed and lengthened; suffixes/enclitics alternate atonic-tonic-atonic... counting from the base; a few suffixes inherently stressed; loans re-parsed as base+atonic suffix; stress change 'rarely' affects meaning; phrase-level key-syllable stress §2.2.3.4 p.92.
